Harrowgate Bakery Co.: Proper Crunch

Opening1
Objective

What has to change

Make Harrowgate Oven Crisps the meal-deal crisp people see as a better snack that still feels like a treat, with proper crunch.

Win trial through the weekday lunchtime meal deal when the bag goes on shelf in March.

Sources [1] [2] (appendix)2
The real question

Harrowgate goes after the meal deal as the baked treat that never apologises, with proper crunch.

Not the virtue crisp. The bakery's crisp, with proper crunch.

Background

Harrowgate Oven Crisps: baked sourdough, 120 g bag, on shelf in March. 43% of shoppers choose brands on price promotion, so the meal deal is the main route to trial.

Sources [1] [3] [4] [5] [6] (appendix)3
The real question

Promotion moves far more crisp choices than guilt does, so the meal deal is where trial is won.

43%Price promotion drives brand choice
11%Buy the less guilty option
81%Like generous portions without too many calories

43% choose on promotion and only 11% buy the less guilty option, yet 81% want generous portions without too many calories.

Sources [3] [4] [7] (appendix)4
Insight

People feel guilty but choose on taste, so Harrowgate must make 'baked' mean bakery crunch, never diet.

Shoppers feel guilty about snacking but choose on taste, not virtue. Harrowgate should make 'baked' mean the bakery, the sourdough and the crunch, never a diet signal.

Our insight, from the evidence below.

Only 11% buy the less guilty option.

Taste is number one; 59% say health isn't a consideration.

Any 'baked' wording falls under CAP Code Section 15.

Sources [3] [4] [5] [8] (appendix)5
Insight

We are talking to young lunchers who make a crisp part of lunch and pick it on deal, not on virtue.

18-35 office lunchers and students choosing a meal-deal crisp, often on promotion, often snacking in place of a meal.

They want the treat that makes lunch, and they will not trade taste for virtue.

What we want them to do
Delighted and a little cheeky, as if they have found a better snack that still feels like a treat.

Proposition

Proper crunch.

From

The crisp you grab because it's on the deal.

To

The crisp you pick for the crunch.

Why they will believe it

  • Baked sourdough crisps in a 120 g bag, made by a bakery.
  • 81% like generous portions without too many calories.
  • Sound and crunch are a distinctive territory that can drive earned media and sales.

The objection it must beat: A baked crisp will read as diet food, and diet food doesn't win the meal deal. We sell bakery and crunch, not virtue; any fat claim is registered, names its comparator and states the difference per same quantity.

How it runs

The plan makes one word, one bag and one sound work harder than the media list.

  • The word does double duty: describing the bakery process lets 'baked' carry the brand while staying out of nutrition-claim territory.
  • The 120 g bag as hero answers the wish for generous portions visually, so no calorie wording is needed in copy.
  • The 6 sheet and D6 sizes meet the lunchtime decision where promotion usually steers the choice, offering crunch as the reason instead.
Sources [2] [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] [12] (appendix)14

Your brief

What you asked us to do, in your words

  • Make Harrowgate Oven Crisps the meal-deal crisp people see as a better snack that still feels like a treat, with proper crunch.
  • Win trial through the weekday lunchtime meal deal when the bag goes on shelf in March.
Success: The crisp you pick for the crunch.
Sources [1] [2] (appendix)20
The real question

A new baked crisp risks reading as the virtue option in a deal slot that promotion and familiar brands control.

  • Promotion steers crisp choice at the weekday lunchtime meal deal, which favours brands shoppers already know.
  • 'Baked' falls under CAP Code Section 15, so the word carries nutrition-claim weight and rules.
  • Few shoppers buy the less guilty option, so a health-coded crisp is easy to walk past.
  • The category leader owns attention with celebrity spoof; out-shouting it is not Harrowgate's route.
Sources [3] [4] [5] [11] [12] [14] (appendix)21
Territories

Territory: Hear It Before You Taste It

Make the sound of the bakery's crunch the brand, so the crisp is known by ear before anyone reads the word 'baked'.

Why it fits
People choose on taste rather than virtue. Leading with crunch puts the treat first and lets 'baked' sit quietly as the reason the bite is so loud. It also stays clear of the diet signal and of nutrition-claim wording. Sound is a distinctive territory a snack brand can own without out-shouting the category leader's spoof humour.
Mood
Close-miked and intimate, then suddenly loud. A quiet office kitchen, a library-hush lunch break or a bus seat, and one bite fills the frame. Mostly silence and texture, little or no voiceover. Warm crust tones on a plain background. The sound carries the joke, not a famous face.
Risks
Ownability is the main risk, because any crisp can claim crunch, so the sound has to be tied to sourdough and the bakery or it becomes generic category noise. Close-mic eating sound divides people, and some find it off-putting. Any line that slides from crunch into 'baked so it's lighter' falls under CAP Code Section 15. The claim that sound drives earned media and sales comes from research and needs confirming before it is used in a selling story.

Lunch, at full volume.

Illustrative, not final
22
Territories

Territory: Baked Means Bakery

Take back the word 'baked' by showing where it comes from: a real bakery, a sourdough, an oven, bakers' hours.

Why it fits
The insight says Harrowgate must make 'baked' mean the bakery and never diet. This route does that literally. Rivals' craft is fryer and kitchen craft, while bakery-made sourdough is a craft no crisp rival holds. It passes the swap test and leaves guilt out entirely.
Mood
Early-morning bakery light, flour in the air, oven doors and proving trays, shot plainly rather than romantically. Matter-of-fact baker's language: weights, times, sourdough. The finished crisp lands in a working lunch, not on a styled table. The sound is ovens, slicing and then the crunch.
Risks
Craft stories can tip into the worn-out 'small batches, hand-made' codes the category already uses, and they can feel precious or premium for a quick meal-deal choice. Bakery cues could pull towards bread and healthier-eating associations, which reopens the diet reading. Every use of 'baked' still sits under CAP Code Section 15, so copy must describe process, not imply nutritional benefit. What can be shown and said about the bakery and its method needs confirming with the client.

Our bakers start with sourdough. You finish with the crunch.

Illustrative, not final
23
Territories

Territory: Picked, Not Grabbed

Show up at the meal-deal moment as the crisp people choose on purpose, because the bag is doing lunch's job and deserves better than whatever is on offer.

Why it fits
Promotion, not guilt, decides the meal-deal crisp, and young lunchers often snack in place of a proper meal. The route turns that habit into a stance: the crisp that makes lunch, picked for its crunch rather than grabbed on deal. It moves the audience from the crisp they grab on the deal to the crisp they pick for the crunch, and it carries no apology for being a treat.
Mood
Deadpan and observational, set at the chiller and the till in the lunchtime rush. Shoppers on autopilot, then one deliberate reach for the bag. Quick cuts, dry on-screen captions, everyday light. The tone is confident and a little cheeky, never preachy about health.
Risks
This route only borderline-passes the swap test, because any meal-deal crisp could say 'pick us on purpose'. It needs the bakery crunch from the other routes to be ownable. It also works against the reality that promotion drives choice, so it may need retailer deal support, and whether that support exists is a question for the client. 'No apology for the treat' must not read as anti-health or encourage replacing meals, which may need care for the secondary lunchbox audience. Any fat comparison must be registered, name its comparator and state the difference per same quantity.

Don't grab it because it's on the deal. Pick it for the crunch.

Illustrative, not final
24
Territories

We recommend 'Baked Means Bakery'

TerritoryWhy (or why not)
Baked Means BakeryIt answers the insight literally by reclaiming 'baked' as bakery and sourdough craft, which is distinctive against fryer-led rivals and keeps guilt out, though it must avoid worn craft clichés and CAP Section 15 implications.
Hear It Before You Taste ItCrunch-first puts taste at the front and sidesteps the diet signal, and sound travels well across video, audio and social, but it is ownable only if tied to the bakery and risks being generic category noise.
Picked, Not GrabbedIt reflects the meal-deal context and taste-led choice, but it only borderline passes the swap test, depends on bakery crunch to be ownable, and works against promotion-driven reality and carries lunch-replacement sensitivities.

How it runs

How we would run it with you

1

Confirm with the client what can be shown and said about the bakery, the sourdough and the method.

2

Confirm where the 120 g bag is listed for the weekday lunchtime meal deal from March, so the trial the work creates can be met.

Write every 'baked' line as process, not benefit. If a fat claim is used, take the registered wording, the comparator range and the same-quantity difference from the client.
